transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Good morning, Mr. Okafor. It is good to see you back in the clinic.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you. I am glad to be home, though I am still struggling quite a bit with my right side.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I want to start by being very direct with you. We made a serious mistake during your admission. You were triaged as low-acuity, which means we didn't recognize the urgency of your stroke symptoms immediately. Because of that, there was a delay in getting you to imaging, and by the time we did the scan, the window to give you thrombolysis—the clot-busting medication—had already closed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The window closed? I remember feeling like I was waiting for hours in that bay. I tried to tell the nurse that my speech was getting worse, but they just said they would be right back.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am deeply sorry. We failed you. As the resident on the team, I take full responsibility for the lack of oversight in your triage process. There is no excuse for this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I spent thirty years teaching history. I know how to analyze a sequence of events. If the medicine is time-sensitive, why was I sitting there? Was it a staffing issue or just a lack of competence?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a failure in our clinical judgment during triage. We missed the signs. Does that explanation make sense to you, or is there any part of that process I can clarify?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It makes sense in a technical way, but it is devastating. My daughter says I’m lucky to be alive, but I feel like I’ve lost a part of my autonomy because of a clerical error.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Do you actually understand? I can't button my own shirt. I can't—

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We really need to focus on the recovery timeline now because I have to go see another patient in a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are rushing me. I am telling you that I am grieving the loss of my dexterity and you are looking at the clock.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I just want to make sure we cover the medical plan before the session ends.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It seems you are more concerned with your schedule than the fact that your team missed the window for my treatment.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Again, I apologize. I am responsible for this. To make sure we are on the same page, you understand that the delay in imaging meant we could not use the thrombolysis drug, correct?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, I understand it. I understood it the first time you said it.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Right. Now, here is exactly how we are going to move forward. First, I have already scheduled a comprehensive swallow and speech evaluation for this Thursday at ten a.m. Second, you will start intensive outpatient physical therapy three times a week starting Monday. Your role is to keep a daily log of your grip strength exercises that I've printed here, which we will review together in two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what is being done to stop this from happening to someone else?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We have already filed a formal incident report and the department is implementing a new mandatory "stroke-screen" double-check for all triage nurses. I am personally presenting this case at our quality improvement meeting tomorrow to ensure the team learns from this error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I appreciate the plan. I just wish the empathy matched the efficiency.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. I’ll see you in two weeks for the follow-up. Let's wrap this up so I can get to my next room.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('I have to go see another patient in a few minutes', 'before the session ends', 'wrap this up so I can get to my next room').

E.justification: Error named in first turn, used lay language ('clot-busting medication'), and checked comprehension twice ('Does that explanation make sense', 'you understand... correct?').

A.justification: Direct apologies used, resident took full responsibility ('I take full responsibility'), and maintained accountability despite patient pushback.

R.justification: Resident uses generic validation ('I understand', 'I hear you') and meets emotional bids with factual redirection to the recovery timeline.

T.justification: Specific steps with timelines (Thursday, Monday), a named patient role (daily log), and prevention addressed (stroke-screen double-check).
